m19.q: predictor-debugger's DESIGN.md says «Written before any dataset, model or prediction exists». Now that you have data, you find a threshold was written wrong. Which change is legitimate?
o: Fix the threshold in the same file and rerun
An amendment at the end of the design with date, reason and commit, and only if the test split has not been evaluated yet
Tweak it until the controls pass
None: a pre-registration is never touched
m19.why: The design allows amendments that are dated, justified and committed, but none after the test has been evaluated. That way anyone can see what changed and when, and nobody tunes a threshold to the result.

m19.q: H14 required a mean ρ ≥ 0.7 with a lower CI ≥ 0.5 on all four networks, and P2gbest got 0.635 [0.413, 0.795]. What was done?
o: Lower the criterion to 0.6 because it was close
Drop P2gbest for being the worst network
Publish H14 as FAIL without touching anything and pre-register a new idea (H17) for round 4
Rerun with another seed until it passed
m19.why: «Nothing was changed to fix it.» The failure was published and led to H17, which was pre-registered separately and passed on all four networks.

m19.q: Why did H14 require its cheap comparator, ΣD3, NOT to meet the same criterion?
o: So the result discriminates: if a simple comparator also meets it, the hypothesis does not show the new check adds anything
To have more hypotheses in the table
Because ΣD3 is a positive control
m19.why: That is why there are three outcomes: PASS, NON-DISCRIMINATIVE (both meet it) and FAIL. A comparator that must fail is a negative control for the hypothesis itself.

m19.q: You change one letter of the hostname inside thresholds.json, without touching any threshold, and run verify.py --saved mac. What happens?
o: Nothing: the thresholds are the same
The verdicts stay the same, but «changed thresholds.json» appears, the fingerprint changes and the command exits with 1
The script crashes with an exception
The verdicts for H1 to H4 change
m19.why: The fingerprint includes the hash of thresholds.json and check_files compares against MANIFEST.sha256. Any changed byte is noticed, even if it does not affect any number.

m19.q: round3/verify.py --saved mac prints H14 … FAIL and still exits with code 0. Why is that correct?
o: It is a bug in the script
The verifier checks that you reproduce what was published (same verdicts and same fingerprint), not that every hypothesis passes
Because the FAIL only counts on the Mac
m19.why: Reproducing a published failure is still reproducing. The exit code says whether your result matches the saved one, not whether the experiment went well.

m19.q: When regenerating the data, no file from WAR, GUERRA or Linux came out bit-for-bit identical to the Mac's (max 8.9e-16). Which conclusion is correct?
o: You must require identical bits and repeat
The Mac files stay canonical, the difference is reported, and what is compared across machines is verdicts and fingerprints, which match
Keep the machine with the smallest difference
m19.why: Bit-identical is not the same as verdict-identical. A difference on the order of float64 epsilon is reported, not hidden, and it does not change any verdict.

m19.q: cluster_bootstrap resamples whole trajectories, not individual steps. Why?
o: Because steps from the same trajectory depend on each other; resampling them one by one treats correlated data as independent and gives a misleadingly narrow interval
Because scipy does not allow resampling steps
Because it makes the CI come out higher
m19.why: The independent unit is the trajectory. With 2,000 replicates and a fixed seed (20261024), the interval reflects how much the result would change with other trajectories.

m19.q: Your three machines give the same fingerprint. What can you write in the README?
o: That the result is independently verified
That the result reproduces in those environments, and that since they are yours it is not an independent reproduction
That no more testing is needed
m19.why: That is what predictor-debugger says in its Limits. «Reproduced» and «reproduced by a third party» are different claims, and an honest report keeps them apart.

o: Putting hypotheses and thresholds in a commit before generating the data
Saving the results at the end
m19.why: That way you cannot move the goalposts after seeing the result.

m19.q: H14 required ≥ 0.7 on all 4 networks and one got 0.635. What do you do?
o: Report that H14 failed, change nothing, and study why
m19.why: The failure gets published; in predictor-debugger it was the seed of H17.

m19.q: What is a fingerprint like EEC9-09E0-F77D for?
o: It summarizes the verdicts: if it matches on another machine, the verdicts match; if anything changes, it changes
m19.why: Comparing a short fingerprint is easier and stricter than eyeballing tables.

m19.q: You regenerate the data on Windows and it differs from the Mac's by 8.9e-16. Conclusion?
o: It is not bit-identical, but the verdicts and the fingerprint match; that is why there are canonical files
m19.why: Bit-identical is not verdict-identical. You declare it and compare what matters.

m19.q: You ran everything on three machines of your own. How do you describe it?
o: Reproducible on my machines; not independent

m19.q: Why include comparators that should fail?
o: To check that the test tells apart the expected cases: testing the tester
m19.why: If the bad comparator also “passes”, the test does not discriminate.

o: Run with the exact versions from the lockfile
m19.why: Pinned environment: the same Python and library versions on every machine.

m19.q: You download a data tar. What do you check before extracting it?
o: Its hash against SHA256SUMS and that it has no absolute paths, “..” or links
m19.why: Integrity and safety before touching the disk.

m19.q: What is “writing down what would contradict you”?
o: Listing the results that would overturn your conclusion: a blind test, another regime, another person with another fingerprint
m19.why: A claim that cannot fail says nothing.

m19.q: A teammate suggests adjusting the threshold “just a tiny bit” after seeing a hypothesis fail by 0.065. Your answer?
o: No: the failure is reported; if there is a better threshold, it gets pre-registered for the next round
I do it without saying so
m19.why: The size of the adjustment doesn't matter: moving the goalposts afterwards voids the pre-registration.

m32.q: The spec says «weekly window (e.g. Aug 20 – Sep 27)». What do you do before building?
o: Schedule the count every 7 days and move on
Count the days in the example (there are 38) and ask what «a week» means for this system
Use the range as is, because the owner wrote it
Wait for the acceptance tests to catch it
m32.why: This is F06. Every weekly count depends on what a week is. It was caught by counting the days in the example, without a single line of code.

m32.q: Three acceptance tests require a spend of $0.2087 ± $0.01, a noise rate of 67% and a P50 between 200 and 250 ms. What is the problem?
o: They copy the numbers from one week of the demo: with real data they fail even if the system works, or pass even if it doesn't
m32.why: F10. A test has to check behavior. The proposal was a test with 10 fixed signals that checks the JSON contract and the escalation rules.

m32.q: The dashboard shows 85% of signals as «threat» and 67% as «noise», and the two classes are mutually exclusive. What do you conclude?
o: That there is a lot of noise
That both numbers cannot be true at once: with 67% noise there are at most 683 signals that are not noise, yet 1,753 threats are reported
That the threshold must be raised
That the model is badly trained
m32.why: F02. Mutually exclusive percentages of the same total cannot exceed 100%. check_numbers.py flags it with ✗.

m32.q: check_numbers.py prints «!» on F01 and F08. What does that mean?
o: That the check could not be run
A number that may be true but is not explained; the script exits with 1 while any remain
m32.why: ✗ is a contradiction and ! is «unexplained». Both leave the exit code at 1, because both need an answer from the owner before building.

m32.q: What does it mean for a finding to be Blocking in this case study?
o: That it is the most expensive to fix
That nobody can build or test that part until someone answers
That an automated tool found it
m32.why: That is the case's scale. And the repo states in its Limits that severity is the reviewer's judgment, not a measurement.

m32.q: The spec sets a 0.85 threshold on the LLM classifier's probabilities. What do you ask for?
o: Raise it to 0.9 to be safe
A calibration plan with a labeled set: in the case, the owner labels about 100 signals and precision is measured with them
m32.why: F13. A threshold on uncalibrated probabilities says nothing. Phase P2 has «precision measured, not assumed» as its gate.

m32.q: In a copy of check_numbers.py you change WEEK_SPEND to 0.40 and F08 comes out ✓. What did you learn?
o: That the 0.40 spend is now explained
That the F08 check has a blind spot: it only flags when the spend matches the classifier input; that mutant survives and must be published
That the script is broken and useless
That the 0.002 tolerance must be lowered
m32.why: That is the WAR idea: the reviewer is a guard too. A survivor in your own check is a finding, not an embarrassment.

m32.q: You notice the spec was built from another company's demo. What changes?
o: Its numbers are examples, not requirements, and every copied figure becomes a question for the owner
You must build it the same as the demo
m32.why: It is the first step of the process: knowing where the spec came from. In the case, that observation explains a good part of findings F01 to F10.

m32.q: The spec announces 14 competitors, lists 12, and the graph draws 7. Which family of problems does this fall into?
m32.why: It is F05: three different figures for the same thing within the same spec.

m32.q: What is the gate for phase P1 of the case study's plan?
o: The 10-fixed-signal test that checks the JSON contract and the escalation rules
m32.why: A verifiable gate replaces the tests that copied a week of someone else's data.

o: A case that must pass (the exact solver, the clean case), to check that the check doesn't raise false alarms
m24.why: If the positive control fails, the problem is the check.

o: A sabotaged case that must fail, to check that the check detects
m24.why: If the negative control passes, the check is asleep.

m24.q: The oracle returns NaN. Correct verdict?
o: Neither PASS nor KILLED: the oracle is invalid
m24.why: NaN is never PASS, and it doesn't prove the mutant died either.

m24.q: The oracle throws an exception on a mutant. Does it count as KILLED?
o: No: an oracle exception is not a killed mutant
m24.why: The mutant died from a harness failure, not because the check detected it.

m24.q: The runner reported oracle_valid: true with the oracle failing (finding 8). Lesson?
o: Test the harness itself, not just what it measures
m24.why: The harness is a guard too, and it gets tested too.

m24.q: Why must the oracle not share a solver with the implementation?
o: Because it would share its bugs and not detect them
m24.why: An independent oracle can disagree; one that shares code can't.

m24.q: The tiny mutation of the RC circuit survives at a 10⁻⁶ tolerance. What do you do?
o: Lower the tolerance until it dies
Report it SURVIVED: the tolerance was frozen beforehand and the survivor stays visible
m24.why: Lowering the tolerance after seeing the result is moving the goalposts.

m24.q: 84 variants: 27 PASS, 54 KILLED and 3 SURVIVED. Kill rate?
m24.why: The 27 PASS are baselines and don't count: 54 / (54 + 3).

m25.why: Whatever flows into a small piece of fluid has to flow out.

m25.q: P3b injects energy. Which check should flag it?
m25.why: Kinetic energy can only decay through viscosity.

m25.q: Why is D4 not a check of the debugger?
o: Because it compares against the exact reference, which doesn't exist in real use; it only serves to judge the debugger
m25.why: DESIGN.md keeps it separate: D4 measures the debugger, it doesn't replace it.

m25.q: What is being tested in predictor-debugger?
o: That the debugger tells the controls apart: a bad network is an acceptable result
m25.why: Pure WAR: you test the tester.

o: In the rollout the network uses its own outputs and errors accumulate
m25.why: That is why H14 failed: summing error sizes didn't capture where they were drifting.

o: Whether two variables rank the same way (rank correlation)
m25.why: It tells you whether a check correctly ranks which predictions are worse.

m25.q: Why bootstrap by trajectories and not by steps?
o: Because steps in a trajectory depend on each other; resampling steps gives narrower, misleading intervals
m25.why: You resample the independent unit, not its pieces.

m25.q: 27 hits out of 29. How do you report it?
m25.why: With 29 cases the interval is wide, and you have to say so.

m26.q: A Lean proof compiles without errors. Which of these does Lean NOT guarantee?
o: That every step of the proof is valid
That the verified statement is the intended one and that the published evidence is what was produced
That the kernel checked the proof
That there are no type errors
m26.why: Lean checks the steps. How it was compiled, whether the statement is the intended one, whether it matches the Clay text and whether the evidence is real are left out: that is what the QA protocol covers.

m26.q: Comparator rejected the statement with «n + 1 ≤ p» instead of «n < p». What does that mean?
o: That the new theorem is false
That the statement changed form; to Lean both are the same by definition, and knowing whether it is equivalent, weaker or false needs a second route
That the original proof is wrong
m26.why: Comparator compares the exact form of the statement. In the Mathlib controls it rejected all 8 changes, including 4 equivalent ones. Rejected means «changed», not «false».

m26.q: What is the comment-only control for, alongside the six statement mutants?
o: To show the verifier doesn't reject everything: a change that doesn't alter the statement must be accepted
m26.why: A positive result alone doesn't distinguish an exact check from one that rejects anything. The control that must pass is the other half of the experiment.

m26.q: The Lean kernel and nanoda accept the same proof. What can you NOT conclude?
o: That two different implementations checked it
That the proof uses only the allowed axioms
That there is no undiscovered kernel bug affecting both
m26.why: In July 2026 a Lean bug and a nanoda bug let the same false proof through. Agreement between two kernels says nothing about unknown bugs.

m26.q: Build B3 looked clean and had 7 precompiled dependencies. How was it discovered?
o: By comparing the .olean timestamps with the build start time
Because it took less time than usual
m26.why: The log didn't show it. An artifact older than the start of the build was not compiled there. That is why B4 exists, with lake --no-cache build.

m26.q: A receipt names a log that exists, but that log is from another run. Which check detects it?
o: P6, which checks that the log exists
Comparing the log with the hash recorded when the step ran
m26.why: It is case 2 of receipt-check: the old log passes P6 and the published procedure exits with 0 and the same output. Only the hash check detects the missing log and the substituted one.

m26.q: Why does an equivalence from the second route only count if it passes the dependency guard?
o: Because the guard speeds up Lean
Because two true statements are trivially equivalent; if the equivalence proof uses the theorem under test, it proves nothing
Because that way Comparator accepts the case
m26.why: The guard checks the transitive dependencies (1,485 constants in the primes case) and deliberately rejected a rigged proof that used Nat.exists_infinite_primes.

m26.q: experiments/mathlib-controls/verify.py prints «PASS: 11 cases match the pre-registered classes». What did you just check?
o: That Lean recompiled the 11 cases on your machine
That the published records match their receipts and that the recomputed classes are the pre-registered ones
m26.why: The script itself says so: it checks the records against their receipts, it doesn't rerun Lean. Saying exactly what was recomputed and what was only verified by hash is part of honest reporting.

m26.q: Comparator rejects a mutated statement. What does it mean?
o: That the statement changed from the challenge's
m26.why: Rejected is not false: even the equivalent mutants were rejected.

m26.q: What is the comment-only control for?
o: To check that a change that doesn't alter the statement is accepted: the guard doesn't raise false alarms
m26.why: It is the verifier's positive control.

m26.q: What do you check with #print axioms?
o: Which axioms the proof uses; a sorryAx would give away an incomplete proof
m26.why: Only propext, Quot.sound and Classical.choice were allowed.

m26.q: A “clean” build received 7 precompiled dependencies. How was it uncovered?
o: By comparing the .olean timestamps with the build start
m26.why: A clean build cannot have artifacts older than its own start.

m26.q: What does scientific-qa-evidence claim about Navier–Stokes?
o: That it is a QA reproduction of published proofs and proves nothing new

m31.q: In predictor-debugger round 5, what does the person preparing the traps send BEFORE handing over the pairs?
o: The pairs and the labels together
Only the SHA-256 of their etiquetas.json
A list with the proportion of traps
Nothing: everything is handed over at the end
m31.why: Step 4 of the kit: only the hash, before handing over anything else. That way the labels can't be changed later without it showing.

m31.q: Why does etiquetas.json have a «sal» (salt) field of 32 random hex characters?
o: So nobody can guess the labels by trying possible labelings until hitting the published hash
m31.why: An unsalted hash of predictable content can be guessed by trial. With a random salt, the hash commits without revealing.

m31.q: The pair ids are 0001, 0002, 0003… and the traps come first. What is the problem?
o: The order leaks the label: the kit asks for random ids (secrets.token_hex(4)) unrelated to the label or the order
m31.why: If the reviewer can infer the label from the name or the order, the test is no longer blind.

m31.q: What does the person running the debugger freeze and upload with a timestamp before opening the pairs?
o: The decision rule and the thresholds
m31.why: Step 6 of the kit. The commitment goes both ways: the traps can't change, and neither can the rule that judges them.

m31.q: An energy trap of ×1.0001 falls below the detection floor and the debugger doesn't flag it. What gets reported?
o: It is removed from the set because it was too small
It is reported as undetected, with its type and magnitude
The thresholds are lowered and it is rerun
m31.why: The kit says so: anything below the floor is reported as undetected, not hidden. Lowering the threshold after seeing the labels would break the blinding.

m31.q: In blind-faults, why was the seed generated with openssl rand -hex 16 outside the assistant's session, with only its hash published?
o: So that nobody, including the assistant running the checks, knew the fault assignment before recording the results, and so that any seed change would show
Because Python doesn't generate random numbers
m31.why: Rule 2 of SEED_COMMITMENT.md. The repo admits the assistant had disk access, so the rule rests on the commitment, and the published hash makes any change detectable.

m31.q: You reveal the seed and want to prove the assignment was the committed one. What do you do?
o: Run shasum -a 256 on the seed, regenerate with assign.py in a separate folder and diff against key.json and the published cases
Ask someone else to trust you
m31.why: It is the recipe in RESULTS.md: if the hash matches and the regeneration comes out byte-for-byte identical, the assignment was the committed one.

m31.q: A blind benchmark came out well, and later a review found 17 problems in its evaluator. What did scientific-qa-evidence do?
o: Kept v1 with an erratum, fixed the evaluator in a v2 and presented it as a regression benchmark, not as a real detection rate
Repeated the experiment until there were no problems
m31.why: A blind test can have defects too. The honest thing is to keep them visible and narrow what is claimed.

m31.q: In a blind test, when is the hash of the labels committed?
m31.why: Afterwards it no longer proves anything.

m31.q: What is the salt in a hash commitment for?
o: So nobody can guess the labels by trying combinations against the hash
m31.why: Without salt, a small set of possible labels can be brute-forced.

m31.q: The file is revealed and its SHA-256 doesn't match the committed one. Conclusion?
o: The blind test is void: the labels changed after the commitment
m31.why: The commitment exists precisely to detect that.

m12.q: Your audit runs green on your laptop and in your CI, but the person who tried to reproduce it didn't get the same fingerprint. Does it pass?
o: Yes, because it works for you
No: the criterion is that someone else reproduces it in a clean environment with the same fingerprint; their report is published as is and the difference is investigated
Yes, if the difference is small
m12.why: The capstone's test is reproduction by someone else. A different result is useful too, but until it matches or is explained, the package does not pass.

m12.q: You want the AI assistant to never push to main. Where do you put the rule?
o: In a PreToolUse hook that exits with exit 2, with an attack suite that tries to sneak past it (like the 28 cases in war-paradigm 03)
m12.why: Hard rules live in code. The hook is a guard too and gets tested too: chained commands, refspecs and a bare push.

m12.q: Your mutant run gives 4 KILLED, 1 SURVIVED and 2 INFRA_ERROR. What is the kill rate?
m12.why: Only KILLED and SURVIVED score: 4 / (4 + 1). INFRA_ERROR shows up in the report but counts neither for nor against.

m12.q: A mutant survives and it is a real product bug (like self-grant in war-paradigm 02). What do you do with it?
o: Remove it so the suite stays green
Keep it visible in the ledger and red in the report, and a strict mode (MUTANT_LAB_STRICT=1) fails the run
m12.why: The survivor is the finding. Hiding it turns the audit into a false green.

m12.q: The reproduction was done by an AI assistant on a cloud machine, directed by you. How do you report it?
o: As an AI-operated reproduction under your direction, not independent; this is written in Limits
m12.why: That is what scientific-qa-evidence («Not independent») and predictor-debugger do. Who reproduced it is part of the evidence.

m12.q: Your verify detects a deleted log but lets through an old log with the same name. What do you have?
o: A check that behaves like P6: it checks that the file exists, not that it is the one produced; each receipt must be tied to the hash recorded when the step ran
m12.why: It is case 2 of receipt-check. The «substituted log» mutant survives your guard, and that gets published and fixed.

m12.q: What must the «What was not executed» section of the AI log contain?
o: What was discussed, planned or illustrated but not run, so nobody mistakes it for evidence
m12.why: CODEX_WORK_LOG.md separates what was executed from what was only illustrated. Without that separation, a reader may take a plan for a result.

m12.q: Which of these deliverables meets the WAR axis at level 3 of the rubric?
o: Two different guards (for example, the suite with mutants and the hook with disguised commands), each with a control that must pass and one that must fail, with command and exit code
An LLM judge with no seeded cases
m12.why: Test the tester: a guard is only trustworthy if you saw it shout at something broken on purpose and stay quiet at something correct.

m12.q: What question does your capstone's architecture README answer?
o: How many tests the repo has
What you automated, what you did NOT, and why (risk)
m12.why: The defense is about judgment, not volume: deciding what NOT to automate is half the design.

m12.q: In the defense they ask: “why contract tests here and E2E there?” Which answer passes?
o: Risk-based judgment: contracts for integrations that break silently; E2E for the user's critical flows
“E2E covers everything, the rest is redundant”
m12.why: Each layer targets a different risk. Being able to explain it is what separates “I know tools” from “I design quality”.

m12.q: Which part of the capstone can AI generate?
o: The whole project, reviewing at the end
The mechanical code (steps, POM) with a reviewed diff; the strategy and the risk analysis are yours
Nothing: it is banned in the capstone
m12.why: The capstone shows your judgment augmented by AI: it types the mechanical parts, you decide and review everything.

m12.q: What does a capstone show that 5 separate exercise repos don't?
o: INTEGRATION: risk-based strategy, connected layers (contract→E2E→BDD→CI→perf) and justified decisions in a coherent system
m12.why: Job postings don't ask for “knows Playwright”: they ask you to design quality. Exercises prove tools; the capstone proves judgment.

m12.q: What does a good architecture README contain?
o: Layer diagram + the WHY of each decision + how to run everything with one command
m12.why: The reader (evaluator, interviewer) needs to understand the design in 5 minutes and be able to run it. Everything else is decoration.

m12.q: Which coverage metric best defends your capstone?
o: RISK coverage: which risks you identified and which layer covers each one — with the gaps declared
m12.why: 100% of lines with empty assertions = 0 protection. “These 8 risks, covered like this; these 2, accepted” is an engineering argument.

m12.q: You didn't have time to build the performance layer. What do you do in the delivery?
o: Not mention it and hope they don't ask
Declare it as conscious debt: why it was postponed, what risk stays open and what the plan would be — just like a known issue
Copy a k6 script from the internet the night before
m12.why: The full method applies to your own project: gaps are declared with a plan, not hidden. That is ALSO evaluated — and it counts in your favor.

m12.q: What must the evaluator be able to do with your repo without talking to you?
o: Read the code and trust it
Clone it and run the suite with the README commands, and see the pipeline green in the repo itself
Ask for access to your machine
m12.why: “Works on my machine” doesn't exist in the capstone: reproducibility (CI/CD module) is shown in your own project.

m12.q: In the defense: “your E2E suite takes 12 minutes, is that OK?” Which answer shows judgment?
o: It depends on the context, and showing it: what runs in the PR gate vs nightly, what gets parallelized and which trade-off was chosen
“It can be brought down with more machines”
m12.why: There is no magic number: there are budgets per context and reasoned decisions. The answer with explicit trade-offs is an engineer's.

m12.q: What weighs MOST in the capstone evaluation?
o: The quality of the DECISIONS: well-analyzed risk, explicit trade-offs, and being able to defend every green in your report
The visual design of the report
m12.why: Tools are learned in weeks; judgment is what gets hired. The capstone is your tangible proof of judgment.

m13.q: Which pitch positions the QA+AI profile?
o: “I design quality strategy and supervise AI-generated tests — this repo proves it”
m13.why: Tools and certificates are a commodity; judgment + AI supervision + tangible proof is the differentiator.

m13.q: How do you escalate a contract mismatch to a stakeholder?
o: “Change the service so my test passes”
Evidence (cURL + response) + impact on the consumer + resolution options
A screenshot of the red test
Wait for the daily to bring it up
m13.why: Evidence + impact + options. The test is the detector; the argument is the affected consumer.

m13.q: “Automation is the detector, not the reason; the beneficiary is the consumer.” When communicating a finding:
o: You talk about your tests and their coverage
You talk about the risk and impact for whoever consumes the service; the suite is just how you detected it
You point at the dev who introduced the bug
You ask for budget for more tests
m13.why: Stakeholders care about the business/user impact, not your framework. Always translate.

m13.q: Which portfolio opens the most doors for this profile?
o: 2-3 repos with READMEs that explain DECISIONS (why this layer, this trade-off) + a visible green pipeline
m13.why: The technical interviewer opens the repo: if the README shows judgment, you've already passed the first filter. Certificates are just a complement.

m13.q: Interview: “tell me about the hardest bug you found”. Which structure shows off your judgment?
o: Tell the weirdest bug you remember
Context → how you detected it (evidence) → root-cause analysis → business impact → what you changed so it doesn't come back
Blame the dev who introduced it
Say your suites never let bugs through
m13.why: The full story (detection→cause→impact→prevention) shows the method's whole cycle in 2 minutes. It's your best oral demo.

m13.q: Trick interview question: “do you aim for 100% coverage?” The method's answer?
o: “No: line coverage isn't the goal — I prioritize RISK coverage and can show how I decide it”
m13.why: Answering “yes” gives you away as a scripter; explaining risk coverage with an example gives you away as an engineer. The question exists to separate them.

m13.q: Which LinkedIn headline works for you while you sleep?
o: Specialty + proof: “QA Automation / SDET · Contract Testing & AI-Augmented QA · [your project]”
m13.why: Recruiters search by keywords and technical people click through to the repo. Concrete specialty + visible evidence = both filters passed.

m13.q: Two offers: “QA Automation” and “SDET”. How do you decide what each one is AT THAT company?
o: SDET always pays more, that one
By asking about the actual work: who designs the strategy? Do they build a framework or just cases? Is there code review of tests?
m13.why: Titles vary by company: there are click-through “SDETs” and “QAs” who architect. The right interview questions reveal the real role.

m13.q: First 90 days in a new QA role. What do you do BEFORE proposing big changes?
o: Rewrite the suite to the course standard
Learn the context: contracts, domain risks, why things are the way they are — and earn credibility with small improvements
Point out everything that's wrong in the retro

m13.q: How do you stay current in the QA+AI wave?
o: What you've learned is enough for 10 years
Continuous practice + community (TAU, MoT) + following the agentic/MCP wave with small projects of your own
m13.why: Today's differentiator is tomorrow's standard. The community tells you what's coming; small projects put it in your hands.
